comments.author: wrs

I had a pile of DV tapes containing my in-laws' 8mm home movies we had digitized 20 years ago. For 20 years they sat in a box because I didn't have time to deal with them. Last month I connected the old DV camcorder (Firewire still works!) and had a little conversation with Claude. In no time I had a neat folder full of categorized, labeled video clips. It ran the camcorder to pull in the tapes, wrote a script to break up the 90-minute compilations of 8mm reels by finding the black screens in between, OCRed the titles from said screens, used the titles for the filenames, and sorted into folders by topic.

The in-laws had a blast watching these and sharing them with various descendants. Frankly, without Claude there's no way this would have happened, certainly not while they were still alive!

comments.author: thombles
comments.text:
I have a similar anecdote with more recent tech. I was helping a community group with their website years ago and replaced their ancient CMS with a new Wordpress site. Unfortunately, little snippets of text stored as content entries in the old CMS were the best written record of the organisation’s activities in the prior 15 years.

Not having any better plan (or DB access), I paged through them all and copy-pasted large quantities of text and images into several large RTFs with no consistent formatting or organisation. I was always going to get back to it one day… and now I have. I had DS4 analyse it all and write a script to reproducibly convert it to a clean, ordered HTML page. I emailed it off and now that org has their history back. I promised I could automate it further if they wanted to republish some of it. This tech is helping real people with their information management.

comments.author: jschuster
comments.text:
For me, the root cause is that I see LLM use as unethical (mostly due to the environmental and intellectual property issues involved in training LLMs, but for other reasons as well). But much of the tech industry (including, it seems, the vast majority of employers) are saying "If you want to stay competitive and survive in this industry, you have to use LLMs to create software". So the choice is seemingly (1) use the big unethical thing, or (2) leave the industry.

Coupled with that is the fact that I care deeply about software quality, but LLM-generated code is making many people care even less about quality (or notice it less) than they already did. There's a general sense of "the LLM wrote it, so it's probably good enough". I deeply disagree with that sentiment, but making that argument is increasingly an uphill battle.

I do still enjoy the "programming" task itself, in the sense of writing code to do what I want, both at work and as an infrequent hobby. I've had to use agentic coding at work enough that I can see the value in it, and I definitely don't feel a sense of loss or like I'm being replaced or anything.

If the ethical issues above were resolved, I'd be happy to use LLMs as part of (but not replacing all of) my work as a software engineer. But as it stands, I feel like most tech companies don't share my values in the way that I thought we once did. So I feel stuck, and maybe even a little betrayed.

(Yes, there have always been ethical issues in tech, especially Big Tech, so maybe I was somewhat naive. But somehow this feels like a bigger, more overt shift in values than we've seen before.)

comments.author: tome

On Lobsters-like forums 25 years ago you would find it very common for people to be in favour of violating copyright law, to obtain "pirated" versions of software, music and video. I appreciate that the individuals in question may be different, but it's interesting to me that the attitude has completely changed.

Similarly, since all human activity imposes environmental impact, how does one come to a determination of what human activities one supports and one doesn't?

The quality one is interesting. Using LLMs has increased the quality of the software I write, markedly, primarily in my personal coding time, but also somewhat software I write for work. I understand that this is not the same for everyone, because it depends to a high degree on management (as it ever did).

comments.author: sjamaan
comments.text:
Interesting observations, thanks for adding to the discussion!

Regarding the copyright violations: one can be in favor of pirating content and still be opposed to the LLM-washing of copyrighted material. The difference is due to the power imbalance, unfairness, corporate greed and exploitation.

Large companies would produce e.g. movies and ask obscene amounts of money for what is essentially near free for them to copy (e.g. early in the DVD era a DVD would cost maybe over ten times what it cost at the end of the era while the actual cost of copying or producing a movie hadn't changed much). Note that e.g. the actors already got paid when making the movie. Nowadays I think the tide has turned a bit against piracy because it was always a bit unethical, but at least a streaming service subscription is not that expensive and offers a high number of videos at no additional charge. In some ways it feels fairer. Or maybe it's more normalized.

Similarly, with LLMs, companies take stuff that cost individuals a lot of effort to produce and sell it back to you at a markup by having the LLM regurgitate the material. So they're making large amounts of money off the backs of other people's work without compensating them (note that I'm including the VC money here, because the fact that they can do these things is bringing in additional investments, so IMO it is irrelevant whether they earn this money through investments or actual subscriptions/token usage).

Some other thing to think about: one might be in favor of piracy at the individual level, but still be in favor of having large-scale piracy organizations who earn lots of money on illegally selling copyrighted stuff brought to justice.

The environmental impact is a hard one I still struggle with. Rutger Bregman in his book Moral Ambition has a great example. He says a monk who never bothers anyone, uses only the bare minimum of what he needs and has zero/negative environmental impact is the ideal for some people. However, a person like that would bring nothing to the world. So that person might as well not have existed. Isn't it better to bring a lasting, positive change to the world (think stuff such as ending poverty, or slavery etc), even if that means you have to e.g. fly around the world to spread your message?

comments.author: tome
comments.text:
Right, so if I am to look for what has remained constant in Lobsters-like forums over the decades, one such thing is something like "objection to (the perception of) power imbalance, unfairness, corporate greed and exploitation", to borrow your apposite words. In the past that was achieved by rebelling against copyright law; in the present that is achieved by appeal to copyright law (in each case at least in some circumstances).

That gets closer to the root of the issue: "power imbalance, unfairness, corporate greed and exploitation" are not lenses through which I tend to interpret the world (since I don't find such lenses particularly beneficial), so my view of LLMs doesn't take them deeply into account. That could explain why I have such a different opinion that many others here.

comments.author: erock
comments.text:
So my current employer has us leaning pretty heavily into using code agents for coding tasks.  I don't think we've had enough time to see the technical debt accrue from using LLMs to write code.  I have personally felt the push and pull of writing huge pieces of code with an agent, only to hit limits with what it is able to accomplish without intervention and, much worse, my lost context on the technical details.

This is the piece where enterprise is going to start snapping back.  People want to talk to people that understand the technical implementations during meetings.  Running to an agent to answer the question is inefficient and I've seen the agent just not think about the problem properly and be confidently wrong.  It's not that the agent isn't capable of reading the code and understanding the logic but it doesn't have the domain knowledge of the business or entire system "in their head."

For personal projects, I've decided to put LLMs back into read-mode.  This isn't me relishing life before LLMs, any "productivity" gains are lost when you can't navigate the code to debug or understand how the system works.  I don't always want to play telephone with an agent to learn how a codebase works.  Sometimes I need to read the source-of-truth.  I don't care if people can vibe through the lifetime of a project, they will know and understand less than someone that wrote it themselves.

A huge part of my personal and professional life is to learn new things and grow as a SWE.  The project itself is not the only goal.  Humans value oracles and when you outsource all thinking to a code agent, you are not an oracle.

I'm honestly not worried about coding, neither as a hobby nor a profession.  I do think code agents are addicting and it is causing burnout, fatigue, and a lost sense of purpose. I say this with confidence because I feel it in me as well.

Billing $375/hour for 3 hours work is a fast track to defaulting on your mortgage. You spend too much time finding clients and billing clients. Plus it's hard to keep a small-job pipeline full, so you spend a bunch of time sitting around with no clients. This is fine when you're 25 and you are fine spending a lot of time hiking instead of working and have reasonable tuition loans. It's less fun at 40 with a mortgage.

There are negatives to our industry, especially certain subsets of it, and I personally want to push very hard for us to unionize and tackle those problems, but I think we should keep the reality in mind that we also in certain senses have suddenly a huge amount of work taken off our plates, but are still being paid the same. That’s pretty nice, I guess if you are not willing to use AI then it does suck, but then I don’t know how to help you. I understand the ethical questions and I share some of them, but I also have to look out first for myself and my family. So even if I did think using generative AI made you an evil person, I’d probably still do it simply for the benefits it provides me directly. ... most of us are incredibly well compensated as software engineers, at least in the US. And now a technology comes out that lets you do your very well paid job for a fraction of the effort…


Human beings like to feel that the work they do makes a positive difference.  That's why health care jobs can be incredibly stressful, but people still do them because they get to experience the difference they make in people's lives in a pretty direct way.

Human beings also tend to live in the future.  Our brains tend to focus on the difference we're going to make, the things that we're going to do.

LLM coding tools have collapsed both of these.  It's clear that our skills no longer matter, and our ability to make a difference is dwindling.   Future employment seems dependent on the use of LLM coding tools, and many people perceive these to have enormous negative externalities.

Sure, in an animal sense, a lot of programmers are pretty comfortable right now.   And I'll happily admit that there are plenty of jobs that are meaningless and pay badly, assuming you can find employment at all.  But I don't think it's strange that people experience a profound loss of meaning.

comments.author: adamshaylor
comments.text:
You’re making a lot of assumptions.

First, you’re assuming that the benefits of any productivity gains of vibecoding go straight to the developer. If vibecoded software was an unalloyed market good, the market would not just take the task of programming off the developers’ plates, it would take the developers off their employers’ plates. Even marginal productivity gains made by technological advances eventually get translated into lower costs for customers, owners, and/or investors. Only a scarcity of actual skills combined with demand for software that actually works keeps software engineers well paid.

Lest anyone accuse me of clinging to a dead craft, I have always sought to write myself out of my job because doing so has always lead to more interesting jobs, at least until now. I have long prepared myself for the possibility that software as a trade might one day be “done.” But that is not what is happening.

This leads to your second assumption: you seem to have fallen into the inevitability trap. But vibecoding is no more the inevitable mode of software engineering than chemical weapons were of warfare. Most vibecoded software appears to disposable at best. We should not expect this to get much better. After all, when has any proclaimed silver bullet turned out to be one?

Finally and anecdotally, I know several software engineers who came from the service industry or the arts where they were making peanuts. Most were the first (and often only) members of their family to get a college education. As they stared down the barrel of impoverished middle age with student loans still hanging over their heads, they got into the software industry through code camps. For a few years, it was good. They had middle class jobs. It was isolating and stressful work, but it was interesting and even fun. It was also the most power they’d ever had in an employer/employee relationship.

Everything changed when they got fed into the industrial press that squeezed them between move-faster-because-LLMs and you-still-own-the-commit-and-its-bugs. Nearly all of them have been deeply anxious and unhappy ever since. (The exceptions are ex-professional musicians, which is interesting, but another topic.) Most are seriously considering quitting tech without anything to fall back on except a vague notion that they could probably find something in the service industry again. If vibecoding has freed you up to finish early and go to the beach, that is indeed a privilege, but not one I myself have encountered, nor do I trust that it can last for very long.

comments.author: enobayram
comments.text:
There's a lot I can relate to in this post, but I think there's a crucial point that often gets missed in analyses like this. As software developers, we analyze this situation as a case of us vs them (i.e. management), but in reality, the management also has as much to worry about in all this as we do.

If LLMs can completely replace software developers, then many of the companies we work for are also at an existential risk. In particular, companies that provide software services and products. Perhaps, before long, a lucky vibe coder with the right setup will pull the arm and the slop-machine-3000-ultra will spit out a great competitor. Software shops are equally afraid of losing their moats, just like software developers do as individuals.

And even if management in a particular software shop isn't afraid of losing their moat themselves, they will have a hard time finding investment, since the investors have to worry whether they'd be burning money on something that next year's LLMs can just be made to write from a single prompt. That single prompt can just be "make a competitor to company X". I actually think that as of 2026, this freezing effect on investment (combined with the brutal macroeconomic environment) might be the main factor in determining the bargaining power and the everyday experience of a software developer.
